lesson.title: Slicing the Cone: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, and Hyperbolas
lesson.summary: Circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas are all conic sections, curves produced by slicing a cone at different angles, and each has a standard equation you can recognize once you complete the square.
lesson.body:
The four conic sections, the circle, the ellipse, the parabola, and the hyperbola, are called that because each one can be produced by slicing a double cone with a flat plane at a particular angle. A slice parallel to the base gives a circle, a slightly tilted slice gives an ellipse, a slice parallel to the cone's slanted side gives a parabola, and a slice that cuts through both nappes of the double cone gives a hyperbola. What matters for the ACT is recognizing each curve from its equation and reading off key features like center, radius, or axis lengths.

A circle centered at (h, k) with radius r has the equation (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², which is really just the distance formula in disguise: it says every point (x, y) on the circle is exactly r units from the center. An ellipse centered at (h, k) has the equation (x - h)²/a² + (y - k)²/b² = 1, where a and b describe how far the ellipse stretches horizontally and vertically from the center. A parabola, depending on orientation, has an equation like y = a(x - h)² + k (opening up or down) or x = a(y - k)² + h (opening left or right), with vertex at (h, k). A hyperbola looks similar to an ellipse's equation but with a minus sign instead of a plus: (x - h)²/a² - (y - k)²/b² = 1, and that single sign change is what turns a closed oval into two open branches.

Recognizing which conic you're looking at often requires rewriting a messy general equation into one of these standard forms by completing the square. Take the equation x² + y² - 6x + 4y - 3 = 0. Group the x-terms and y-terms: (x² - 6x) + (y² + 4y) = 3. To complete the square on x² - 6x, take half of -6 (which is -3), square it (getting 9), and add 9 to both sides. To complete the square on y² + 4y, take half of 4 (which is 2), square it (getting 4), and add 4 to both sides. This gives (x² - 6x + 9) + (y² + 4y + 4) = 3 + 9 + 4, which factors to (x - 3)² + (y + 2)² = 16. This is a circle centered at (3, -2) with radius √16 = 4, since the sums 9 and 4 turn each grouped expression into a perfect square binomial, exactly the technique used for solving quadratic equations.

Ellipses reward the same kind of careful reading once they're in standard form. Consider 4x² + 9y² = 36. Dividing every term by 36 gives x²/9 + y²/4 = 1, which matches the ellipse form with a² = 9 and b² = 4, so a = 3 and b = 2. Since a is under the x² term and a > b, the ellipse stretches farther along the x-axis, reaching from x = -3 to x = 3, while it only reaches from y = -2 to y = 2 vertically. Its foci, two special points used in the ellipse's geometric definition, lie along that longer axis at a distance c from the center, where c² = a² - b² = 9 - 4 = 5, so c = √5, about 2.236, giving foci at (√5, 0) and (-√5, 0). Being able to move fluidly between a messy equation and this kind of geometric picture is the core skill this topic tests.
